topic: Design research for the blog / writing section of satishregonda.in — index and post-page design, reading experience, discovery, math/figures/citations, and voice — based on ~38 successfully fetched writing-first personal sites, academic blogs, and editorial magazines.
key_findings: The dominant pattern among the best writing-first sites is a DATE + TITLE + ONE-LINE DEK list — not cards, not grids, not thumbnails. Craig Mod's essay index (https://craigmod.com/essays/) is literally 'August 2026 / A Swarm of Blood Robots / Recent adventures using LLMs' repeated 70+ times, 2009–2026. Karpathy (https://karpathy.github.io/) is the same: date, title, one-line description, ~40 posts on one page, no pagination, no tags, no reading time, no search. Every image-card blog index I looked at belonged to a magazine with a staff, not a person.

The authored one-line dek is the single highest-leverage element for a small blog. Karpathy, Craig Mod, Ben Kuhn ('Related' items each carry a tagline), Chris Olah (thumbnail + descriptive subtitle), and Works in Progress all pair every title with a human-written line. Auto-generated excerpts (first 30 words) are the giveaway of a template. This must be a required field in the professor's authoring flow, not optional.

Low-volume blogs solve 'looks empty' with CURATION, not filler. Ben Kuhn (https://www.benkuhn.net/) leads with ~10 featured essays and deliberately shows NO dates on the index (timelessness), then links to '/recent' for chronology. Nadia Asparouhova (https://nadia.xyz/) shows exactly 3 'Recent Posts' plus 5 'Favorites'. Matt Might (https://matt.might.net/articles/) offers three entry points: Newest / Random / Chronological. None of them show a count.

Bartosz Ciechanowski (https://ciechanow.ski/) publishes roughly one post a year and the site never reads as abandoned. The mechanism: enormous per-post depth, a visible dated finish line ('December 17, 2024'), an 'Archives' link implying history, and zero engagement furniture. Depth substitutes for frequency. This is the closest model to a professor posting 3–4 times a year.

Chris Olah (https://colah.github.io/) groups ~30–40 posts by SUBJECT DOMAIN rather than date ('Neural Networks (General)', 'Recurrent Neural Networks', 'Visualizing…'), and adds an explicit 'Rough Notes' section for lower-polish material plus a 'Traditional Papers' list at the bottom. Naming a lower tier ('rough notes') removes the pressure that kills low-frequency blogs.

Tufte CSS (https://edwardtufte.github.io/tufte-css/) restricts the whole system to THREE heading levels — h1 title, h2 section, h3 subsection — justified by the Feynman Lectures covering all of physics in 1800 pages with two levels. Its palette is off-white #fffff8 on off-black #111111, ETBook with Palatino/Georgia fallback. Sidenotes are a label+checkbox pair (`margin-toggle sidenote-number` → `span.sidenote`), margin notes are the same unnumbered (`marginnote`), and on narrow screens they collapse behind the checkbox — no JavaScript at all.

Gwern's design page (https://gwern.net/design) gives named, defensible choices: Source Serif Pro + Source Sans Pro for text, IBM Plex Mono for code (picked after a blind comparison of ~20 code fonts because a slashed zero was a hard requirement), sidenotes.js by Said Achmiz (MIT) that swaps sidenotes for floating footnotes when the window narrows, and — critically — DARK MODE USES PER-IMAGE AI CLASSIFICATION (InvertOrNot.com) to decide whether to invert, because blanket inversion destroys figures.

Distill (https://distill.pub/2016/misread-tsne/) uses a narrow centred text column (~600–800px) with figures escaping to full-bleed, numbered inline citations resolving to a References block, an author + affiliation + date byline, and an explicit 'Citations and Reuse' block containing plain-text citation, BibTeX, CC licence, and a link to the GitHub source. The BibTeX block is the single most 'academic' affordance available and almost no personal site has it.

Simon Willison (https://simonwillison.net/) shows WORD COUNT, not reading time — '[2,270 words]' on each long entry. He also runs the most complete discovery layer I found: 1,000+ tags with counts on https://simonwillison.net/tags/, tag intersection via /tags/tag1+tag2/, year archives 2002–2026, and `<link rel="alternate" type="application/atom+xml" href="/atom/everything/">` in the head. He separates entry types: Entries, Links, Quotes, Notes.

Reading time in minutes is contested and reads as media-company furniture. Baldur Bjarnason's 'A note on estimated reading times' (https://www.baldurbjarnason.com/2024/on-reading-time/) argues it ignores typeface, screen, astigmatism, vocabulary and format skill; the proposed alternative is a plain word count. Of everything I fetched, only Works in Progress (a staffed magazine) shows minutes; Karpathy, Dan Luu, Ciechanowski, Olah, Gwern, Tao, Aaronson, macwright, jvns, Ken Shirriff all show none.

Reading progress bars are a documented designer irritant — Digiday's 'Why designers hate on the article progress bar' (https://digiday.com/media/designers-hate-article-progress-bar/) reports they are distracting outside long-form and are confused with loading bars. Zero of the ~25 personal/academic sites I fetched had one. It is a reliable tell that a site was built from a template.

Julia Evans' post pages (https://jvns.ca/blog/2026/05/15/moving-away-from-tailwind--and-learning-to-structure-my-css-/) carry only a date and ONE category tag at the top, a ~950px content column, h1 for title and h3 for sections, prev/next links at the bottom, a weekly-digest offer placed mid-page, and no comments. Her index is 'Most recent 10 posts' followed by ~20 thematic groupings (Git, DNS, Terminals, Career…) with ★ marking popular posts.

Academic blogs still use categories + comment counts + monthly archives, and they still get read. Terence Tao (https://terrytao.wordpress.com/) shows date, categories ('expository', 'math.CA'), tags, author and comment count, renders LaTeX as images via the WordPress plugin, truncates with 'Read the rest of this entry »', and cites via zbMATH and arXiv links. Scott Aaronson (https://scottaaronson.blog/) publishes FULL posts on the index with a sidebar carrying monthly archives back to 2005, 30+ categories, a blogroll, lecture notes, and a 'The Basics' block (CV, papers, talks).

The closest disciplinary comparators are RealClimate (https://www.realclimate.org/) and the EGU Hydrological Sciences blog (https://blogs.egu.eu/divisions/hs/). RealClimate has a 'Start here' nav item, a recurring monthly open thread ('Unforced Variations'), and footer sections for 'Data and Graphics', 'Index', 'Acronym Index'. EGU HS runs 34 categories (groundwater, catchment hydrology, extreme events, hydrological forecasting, remote sensing, water policy), author + date + featured image + excerpt, and post types that map exactly to this professor's mix: event explainers ('Summary of the August 26th, 2026, Himalayan flash flood'), method notes ('eDNA4Hydrology'), and field-of-view opinion ('Has groundwater finally gone mainstream?').

Titles from credible academic bloggers are declarative claims or genuine questions, never benefit promises: 'A Recipe for Training Neural Networks' (Karpathy), 'Against "Brain Damage"' (Mollick), 'Has groundwater finally gone mainstream?' (EGU HS). Openings state provenance or occasion rather than hooking: Karpathy opens 'Some few weeks ago I posted a tweet…'; Aaronson opens 'I woke up yesterday with the following thoughts, which are probably either obvious or dumb.' Admitting uncertainty is the credibility move.

Editorial magazines earn their look through the DEK, not the layout. Asterisk (https://asteriskmag.com/) writes deks that frame rather than summarize — 'Once you realize what that means, you'll be giving two cheers for the American work ethic'. Works in Progress (https://worksinprogress.co/issue/the-world-of-tomorrow/) opens with 'When the future arrived, it felt… ordinary. What happened to the glamour of tomorrow?' A one-line summary of the post's contents is not a dek.

Measure and size have a settled answer: 50–75 characters per line with ~66 as the sweet spot, WCAG 1.4.8 capping at 80, body text 16–20px, line-height ~1.5 (UXPin, Baymard, Google Fonts Knowledge). At 19–20px serif that lands at roughly 660–700px of text column.

KaTeX vs MathJax: KaTeX renders synchronously with no reflow and a smaller bundle with faster font loading; MathJax 3 has closed much of the speed gap and supports far more LaTeX plus MathML output for screen readers. For a hydrology blog with occasional equations, KaTeX rendered AT BUILD TIME ships zero runtime JS and is the clear choice; MathJax's advantage only matters for exotic macros.

Ken Shirriff (https://www.righto.com/) shows the right treatment for photograph-heavy technical posts: every image is hyperlinked to a full-resolution version, captions sit below with a source attribution, and numbered endnotes at the article end are bidirectionally linked back into the text. This is exactly what field notes from flood sites need.

OG cards matter and should be generated, not hand-made: 1200×630, built at build time with Satori/Resvg or @vercel/og, and consistency beats artistry ('the best OG image is not the most artistic one'). A generated card with the post title in the site serif on the site's paper ground is both cheaper and more distinctive than a stock photo.
recommendations: SPLIT THE STREAM IN TWO. 'Writing' (essays, prose, permanent, ~4–8/year) and 'News' (one-line dated updates: paper accepted, student defended, talk given, ~2/month, fed from a Google Sheet). The news ticker on the homepage keeps the site visibly alive while the blog matures slowly, and it stops the blog degrading into a feed of 'our paper got accepted' — which is what kills the essay-ness of academic blogs.

DO NOT LAUNCH WITH ZERO POSTS. Seed 3 pieces from material he already effectively has: (1) a rewritten version of his research statement as a first-person essay — 'Why urban flooding is a forecasting problem, not a drainage problem'; (2) an FAQ/advice post for prospective students, which he answers by email dozens of times a year anyway; (3) a short explainer on one recent paper, written for a Telugu/English general reader. Each is ~800–1500 words and can be drafted from existing text in an afternoon.

USE A KIND LABEL, NOT TAGS, AT LAUNCH. Four fixed kinds: 'Explainer' (research made legible), 'Comment' (water policy and practice), 'Field note' (site visits, gauges, floods, photographs), 'For students' (advice and how-to). Render the kind as a small uppercase sans label above each title. Four kinds across three posts reads as an editorial plan; a tag cloud across three posts reads as an abandoned CMS.

INDEX LAYOUT: single-column editorial list, left-aligned, no thumbnails, no cards, no grid. Per entry: kind label (11px uppercase sans, letterspaced, muted) / title (28–34px serif, tight leading) / dek (17–18px, muted, 1–2 lines) / date (14px sans, muted, right-aligned on the baseline of the label or under the dek). Vertical rhythm of ~72–96px between entries with a hairline rule; at three posts this fills a screen and a half without feeling stretched.

BELOW THE THREE ENTRIES, ADD TWO EDITORIAL BLOCKS instead of pagination. First: 'What I write about here' — a short standfirst paragraph in the professor's own voice plus the four kinds with one sentence each. Second: 'Elsewhere' — links to peer-reviewed papers (Google Scholar), the RAFT group page, talks, and press. This makes the page feel authored and gives a visitor somewhere to go when the archive is thin. Retire both blocks once the archive passes ~12 posts.

POST PAGE: 66ch measure (~660–700px) at 19–20px serif with 1.6 line-height, ragged-right (never justify — justified text without proper hyphenation produces rivers and is the classic academic mistake). Only h2 and h3 in the body, per Tufte. Header stack: kind label / title / dek in larger muted italic / a single metadata line reading 'Satish Regonda · 14 March 2026 · 2,300 words'. Word count, not minutes.

NO PROGRESS BAR, NO READING-TIME-IN-MINUTES, NO SOCIAL SHARE ROW, NO SCROLL-TRIGGERED FADE-INS. These four together are the strongest signal that a site was assembled from a template, and none of the ~25 personal or academic sites I fetched has all four. If sharing must exist, a single quiet 'copy link' at the foot of the post is enough.

IMPLEMENT TUFTE-STYLE SIDENOTES, CSS-ONLY, using the checkbox/label pattern so they work without JavaScript. At ≥1200px viewport they sit in the right margin at 14–15px; below that they collapse to an inline toggle. Map Google Docs' native 'Insert > Footnote' straight onto them — this gives the professor a familiar academic affordance that produces a genuinely distinctive layout with zero new skills.

THREE FIGURE WIDTHS, one caption style. `inset` (text width), `wide` (text + ~120px bleed each side, for hydrographs and maps), `full` (edge-to-edge with the caption in the margin band). Captions: 14–15px sans, muted, left-aligned to the figure, prefixed 'Fig. 1 —'. Every raster figure links to its full-resolution version (Ken Shirriff's pattern), which matters enormously for flood-extent maps and time-series plots.

DARK MODE: DO NOT INVERT SCIENTIFIC FIGURES. Wrap every figure in a light 'plate' — a paper-coloured card with ~16px padding, 4px radius and a hairline border — that stays light in both themes. This is honest to how the figure was authored, matches how a printed journal figure looks on a page, and avoids the Gwern problem entirely (he needed an AI classifier precisely because inversion breaks figures). Optionally allow a `data-invert-ok` opt-in for pure black-line schematics.

MATH: KaTeX at build time (rehype-katex or the katex CLI in the pipeline), zero runtime JavaScript, KaTeX CSS inlined. Let the professor type `$...$` and `$$...$$` directly in the Google Doc — it survives Docs→Markdown export cleanly, which the Docs equation editor does not. Reserve MathJax only if he ever needs macros KaTeX rejects; that is unlikely for hydrology.

CITATIONS: for any 'Explainer' post, put a bordered callout immediately under the dek reading 'This post is based on: <full citation> · DOI: <link> · PDF'. At the foot of the post, a numbered 'References' block with DOI links. And borrow Distill's move: a small collapsed 'Cite this post' block containing a plain-text citation and a BibTeX entry. Almost no personal academic site does this and it costs nothing.

PERMALINKS: /writing/<slug>/ with no date in the URL, and the date displayed on the page. Rationale: on a blog publishing four times a year, a dated URL makes an eighteen-month-old post look stale in search results and in shared links, while the content (a flood explainer, advice for students) is evergreen. Slugs kebab-case, ≤5 words, frozen at first publish. Keep a /writing/archive/ redirect map so slugs can be corrected without breaking links.

FEEDS AND EMAIL: ship /feed.xml (Atom), declare it with `<link rel="alternate" type="application/atom+xml">` in the head, and link it visibly in the footer — RSS is still normal in academic and hydrology circles and costs nothing. Add a plain email subscribe (Buttondown, as interconnected.org uses, or a single Google-Form-backed field) with one line of reassurance ('a few times a year, one-click unsubscribe'). Do NOT put the blog on Substack: it would move the writing off satishregonda.in, wrap it in another company's identity, and drop paywall and 'restack' furniture onto a professor's page.

DEFER DISCOVERY MACHINERY UNTIL IT IS EARNED. Tags page: not until ~15 posts. Year-grouped archive page: not until ~25 posts. Search (Pagefind — static, no service, no API key): not until ~40 posts. Pagination: not until ~30 posts; before that, one page holds everything. Shipping a search box over three posts is worse than shipping nothing.

TOC RULE: render a table of contents only when a post has four or more h2 sections. On ≥1200px it becomes a quiet sticky rail in the left margin (14px sans, no numbers, current section in the text colour, others muted); below that a collapsed 'Contents' disclosure placed after the dek. Never a floating pill or an overlay.

SHIP A REAL PRINT STYLESHEET. This is a genuine academic differentiator and almost free: 11pt serif black on white, nav/footer/subscribe hidden, sidenotes promoted to numbered footnotes at the page foot, link URLs printed after link text via `a[href^="http"]::after { content: " (" attr(href) ")" }`, `break-inside: avoid` on figures and tables, and the full citation block printed. Professors print things and hand them to students.

OG CARDS GENERATED AT BUILD, 1200×630: post title set in the site's serif at ~64px on the site's paper background, a hairline rule, and 'Satish Regonda · satishregonda.in' in small sans at the foot. One template, no images, perfectly consistent. Use Satori + Resvg in the build, or a pre-rendered SVG-to-PNG step.

AUTHORING CONTRACT FOR THE GOOGLE DOC. One Doc per post in a /Blog folder. A 2-column table at the very top of the Doc with rows: Title, Dek, Date, Kind, Tags, Slug, Status (Draft | Published). The build reads Status as the publish switch — this is the whole editorial workflow, and it is comprehensible to a non-technical author. Heading 1 in the Doc → h2, Heading 2 → h3 (so he never touches the page title). Docs footnotes → sidenotes. Images placed inline; the paragraph directly beneath an image, styled with the Docs paragraph style 'Caption', becomes the figure caption.

VOICE GUIDANCE TO GIVE THE PROFESSOR, in writing, as three rules: (1) Title with a claim or a real question — 'Hyderabad's floods are a forecasting failure, not a drainage failure', not 'Understanding urban flooding'. (2) Open with provenance or occasion — 'A student asked me this in March and I gave a bad answer, so here is a better one' — never with 'In this post we will explore'. (3) State your uncertainty explicitly; hedging is a credibility signal in this genre, not a weakness. Add a fourth operational rule: no call-to-action inside the body of a post.
details: ## Method I fetched ~38 pages successfully. Failures (do not cite these as verified): `tomacwright.com` (DNS — the real domain is `macwright.com`, which I did fetch), `pgbovine.net` (DNS failed; I fetched `pg.ucsd.edu` instead), **`raftwaters.in` (DNS: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND — the RAFT site is NOT currently resolving; flag this to the team before linking to it)**, `michaelnielsen.org` (returns a "site is almost here" placeholder), `statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu` (HTTP 403), `distill.pub/2020/circuits/zoom-in/` (payload >10MB), `worksinprogress.co/issue/the-conquest-of-cholera/` (404 — that slug does not exist). --- ## 1. Index page design — what the evidence actually shows ### The dominant form: date · title · dek, single column | Site | Index form | Metadata per entry | |---|---|---| | karpathy.github.io | Reverse-chron, one page, ~40 posts, no pagination | Date ("Feb 12, 2026") + title + one-line description. No tags, no reading time, no search. RSS at `/feed.xml`. | | craigmod.com/essays/ | Reverse-chron, 70+ essays 2009–2026, no categories | Month+year / title / one-line italic descriptor. Separate "Popular Essays" block of 4 near the newsletter signup. | | danluu.com | Reverse-chron, split into "Public posts" and "Patreon posts" | MM/YY + title only. No descriptions, no tags. RSS at the bottom. | | macwright.com | Reverse-chron, no year grouping | YYYY-MM-DD + title. Sections split by kind: Writing / Reading / Photos / Projects / Drawings / Micro / About. Auto light/dark toggle. | | jvns.ca | "Most recent 10 posts" then ~20 thematic groups (Git, DNS, Terminals, Career…) | Date + title, ★ marks popular posts. | | colah.github.io | ~30–40 posts grouped by subject domain, not date | Thumbnail + descriptive subtitle. Separate "Rough Notes" tier and a "Traditional Papers" list at the bottom. | | benkuhn.net | ~10 featured essays first, then 30+ recent | **No dates on the index** — deliberate timelessness. | | nadia.xyz | 3 "Recent Posts" + 5 "Favorites" | Minimal. | | matt.might.net/articles/ | Three entry points: Newest / Random / Chronological | Minimal. | | ciechanow.ski | A handful of posts + "Archives" | Date only. No tags, no read time. | | interconnected.org/home/ | Recent posts + archive by year 2000–2026 **with post counts per year** + "Best of" collections + "On this day" | Buttondown email and RSS, both with explainer links for the unfamiliar. | Card grids with hero images appeared **only** on staffed editorial products (Works in Progress, Asterisk, Cal Newport's WordPress theme) and on Maggie Appleton's site — where each card carries a *custom illustration she drew*, not a stock photo. That is the distinction: a card grid is only credible if someone is making the images. ### Curation devices for small archives (directly applicable) - **Ben Kuhn**: featured-first, dateless index, `/recent` for chronology, and at the bottom of each post a "Related" trio each with a one-line tagline ("Staring into the abyss as a core life skill"). - **Nadia**: literally 3 recent + 5 favorites, and the site explicitly frames itself as "a little pied-à-terre" — modest scope stated out loud. - **Robin Sloan** (robinsloan.com): groups by *medium* not chronology (Basics / Archives / Novels / Special Projects), states an entry point in prose ("I encourage you to start with my novels"), uses ★ to mark favoured works, and shows a site "updated" date (September 3, 2026) — which is a clever way to signal liveness when posts are rare. - **Nicky Case** (ncase.me): sections named by verb — "SHTUFF YOU CAN PLAY / READ / WATCH" — and **no dates or metadata at all**. Removing dates removes the staleness problem entirely. - **Chris Olah**: "Rough Notes" as a named lower tier, with the reason stated ("polishing takes lots of time"). ### Editorial magazines — what makes them read as magazines - **Asterisk** (asteriskmag.com): issue-based (Issue 15: "Work"), cover image + TOC on the landing page, print subscription prominent, four issues/year, masthead. Deks frame rather than summarize. - **Works in Progress** (worksinprogress.co): "Spotlight Issues" numbered 26, 25, 24… each with a cover image; article previews carry large hero image + headline + author byline + one-sentence dek + topic tag (Cities, Biotech, Economics) + "Read more →". Secondary "Notes" tier for shorter pieces. - Both derive their magazine-ness from **issue structure + dek voice + a named editorial beat**, not from layout tricks. A personal site can borrow the dek voice and the beat statement without needing issues. --- ## 2. Post page design ### Measure and type - Research consensus: 50–75 characters/line, 66 the cited sweet spot; WCAG 1.4.8 caps at 80; body 16–20px; line-height ~1.5 (UXPin, Baymard, Google Fonts Knowledge, Pimp my Type). - Julia Evans' post CSS uses a **950px** centred column (that includes padding; the text measure is narrower). - Distill's article text column is roughly **600–800px** with figures escaping to full-bleed. - Tufte CSS palette: background `#fffff8`, text `#111111`, ETBook → Palatino → Georgia. - Gwern: Source Serif Pro (body), Source Sans Pro (UI), IBM Plex Mono (code, chosen after a blind comparison of ~20 code fonts specifically because a slashed zero was a requirement). ### Heading hierarchy Tufte CSS restricts to three levels total — `h1` title, `h2` section, `h3` subsection — and justifies it: *"the Feynman lectures write about all of physics in 1800 pages, using only 2 levels of hierarchical headings."* Julia Evans in practice uses h1 for title and h3 for all sections. Karpathy's "Recipe" post uses numbered sections (1–6) with bolded tips as a pseudo-h3 layer. Ethan Mollick uses **bold section headers as cognitive anchors** ("The Learning Brain", "The Creative Brain", "The Collective Brain") — a light, non-numbered structure that suits opinion pieces. ### Sidenotes / footnotes / margin notes - **Tufte CSS**, no JS: `…`. Unnumbered variant uses `marginnote` and a ⊕ toggle. On narrow viewports the note is hidden and revealed by the checkbox. - **Gwern**: `sidenotes.js` (Said Achmiz, MIT) promotes footnotes to sidenotes "when the browser window is wide enough", falling back to floating footnotes on narrow screens. - **Ken Shirriff** (righto.com): numbered endnotes at the article foot, **bidirectionally linked** (superscript → note, note → back to text). Notes carry source citations and technical clarifications. - **Ben Kuhn**'s essays use a top-of-post table of contents plus numbered footnotes (6 in the "Why and how to write things on the Internet" piece). ### Figures - **Tufte CSS** defines three placements: main-column `figure`, **margin figures** (a `figure` inside a `marginnote`), and **full-width figures** via `class="fullwidth"`, plus `iframe-wrapper` for responsive embeds. - **Ken Shirriff**: every image hyperlinked to its full-resolution version; caption *below*, with source attribution and often multi-line ("The core stack from the Spacelab computer. I removed the top board to show the core planes."). - **Distill**: interactive figures extend beyond the text column to full viewport width. - **Ciechanowski**: interactive canvases sit **full-width inline within the prose**, never in a sidebar, and the caption text *precedes* the demo to prepare the reader ("You can drag the planet around to change its position. The arrow symbolizes the initial velocity…"). - **Works in Progress**: images inline in the flow with terse source captions only ("Source: Author's collection", "Source: Wikimedia Commons"). - **Ethan Mollick**: charts minimally captioned inline ("Nigeria study, the grade distribution of those who participated in the AI tutoring sessions (blue) versus those that did not (red)"). ### Blockquotes / pull quotes / epigraphs - Tufte CSS uses `blockquote` with a `footer` for attribution, italicized, for **epigraphs** at the head of a section. - Works in Progress uses indented block quotes for quoted dialogue and source passages. - **No serious personal academic site I fetched used decorative pull quotes.** They are a magazine device; on a one-author site they read as filler. ### Post footers observed - Karpathy: Disqus comments + social links. (Disqus is a wart — third-party tracking on an otherwise clean site.) - Julia Evans: prev/next post links, copyright, related recommendations. No comments. A "Want a weekly digest?" offer appears **mid-page**, not as a modal. - Ben Kuhn: "Related" — three posts each with a one-line tagline, thematically chosen not chronological. - Distill: "Citations and Reuse" with plain-text citation, **BibTeX**, CC licence, GitHub source link, DOI. - Ethan Mollick: subscribe CTAs "discretely at the footer, not prominently interrupting the narrative flow." --- ## 3. Reading experience **TOC.** Distill relies on numbered section headings (1–6) as an implicit TOC. Ben Kuhn puts an explicit hierarchical TOC at the top of long essays. Gwern auto-generates a TOC from headers, and for very large tag pages uses *popup-based* navigation to avoid rendering thousands of entries. Ciechanowski's "Moon" uses major section headers as implicit signposts with no rail. **Progress bars.** Digiday: designers argue they are distracting unless the piece is long-form, they don't make sense on blog posts, and users confuse them with loading bars. Zero of the personal/academic sites had one. **Reading time.** Baldur Bjarnason's argument (baldurbjarnason.com/2024/on-reading-time/): estimates ignore typeface, screen quality, astigmatism, vocabulary familiarity, and format skill. Proposed alternatives from the discussion: raw word count, or word count plus a density note ("850 words, tech jargon, complex sentences"). Simon Willison's practice — `[2,270 words]` — is the clean version. Works in Progress does show reading time; it is a staffed magazine optimising for casual readers. **Scroll behaviour.** Nothing in the reference set uses scroll-jacking, parallax, or reveal-on-scroll. Gwern's stated principles are explicit: "Aesthetically-pleasing Minimalism", "Accessibility & Progressive Enhancement" *requiring no JavaScript for core reading*, "Speed & Efficiency", "Semantic Zoom". **Print.** None of the fetched pages advertised a print stylesheet, which is exactly why shipping one is a differentiator for an academic audience that prints and annotates. --- ## 4. Discovery **Tags.** Simon Willison's `/tags/` lists 1,000+ tags with counts (ai 2,184; python 1,257; javascript 754; django 588; datasette 466; openai 450; claude-code 116), supports **intersections at `/tags/tag1+tag2/`**, and sits above a year archive 2002–2026. Terence Tao shows categories (`expository`, `math.CA`) plus tags plus comment count. Scott Aaronson has 30+ sidebar categories. EGU HS runs **34 categories**. Karpathy, Dan Luu, Ciechanowski and Craig Mod have **no tags at all** and are fine. **Series / entry types.** Simon Willison splits Entries / Links / Quotes / Notes / Guides / Elsewhere (and even Sightings and Releases). macwright.com splits Writing / Reading / Photos / Projects / Drawings / Micro. Maggie Appleton splits Essays / Notes / Patterns / Smidgeons / Talks / Podcasts / Library. RealClimate runs a recurring monthly open thread ("Unforced Variations") — a low-effort series that guarantees a heartbeat. **Archive.** Interconnected shows years 2000–2026 *with per-year post counts*, plus "On this day". Aaronson has expandable monthly listings 2005→present. Kottke has "Archive + Tags" over a 25+ year corpus. **Search.** Gwern has search in a floating toolbar. Simon Willison has it. Karpathy, Dan Luu, Ciechanowski, Olah do not. **RSS/Atom.** Confirmed present at: karpathy (`/feed.xml`), Ben Kuhn (``), Simon Willison (``), Dan Luu, Julia Evans, Ken Shirriff ("follow me on Bluesky… or RSS"), Terry Tao, Aaronson (posts + comments feeds), Kottke, RealClimate, Interconnected. Search results confirm RSS remains in active academic use, alongside Google Scholar Alerts (email, convertible to RSS via RSS Bridge) and Semantic Scholar alerts. **Email.** Craig Mod: mid-page signup, two named newsletters, reassurance copy "Always one-click to unsub". Interconnected: Buttondown + RSS side by side, each with an explainer link. Julia Evans: "Subscribe to a weekly digest of these blog posts" in the sidebar. Ethan Mollick (Substack): subscribe is the first interactive element, 472,000 subscribers, with a "No thanks" dismissal — that aggressiveness is Substack's, not his. **Permalinks observed.** `karpathy.github.io/2019/04/25/recipe/` (date-in-path), `jvns.ca/blog/2026/05/15//` (date-in-path), `worksinprogress.co/issue/the-world-of-tomorrow/` (no date), `benkuhn.net/writing/` (no date), `ciechanow.ski/moon/` (no date, single word). The undated form dominates among low-frequency, essay-shaped writers. **OG/Twitter cards observed.** Ben Kuhn: `og:title`, `og:site_name`, `og:url`, `og:description`, `twitter:card=summary`, `twitter:site=@benkuhn`. Simon Willison: `og:site_name`. Neither uses a generated image card. Current best practice from search: 1200×630, build-time generation via Satori (JSX→SVG) + Resvg (SVG→PNG) or @vercel/og; "the best OG image is not the most artistic one. It is the one that is readable, consistent, and easy to generate every single time." --- ## 5. Math, citations, charts, dark mode **KaTeX vs MathJax.** KaTeX processes synchronously without page reflow, smaller bundle, faster font loading. MathJax 3 has closed much of the performance gap, supports far more LaTeX plus AsciiMath and MathML, and MathML output matters for screen readers. Hybrid (KaTeX by default, MathJax where needed) is a documented pattern. For build-time rendering the accessibility argument weakens since KaTeX emits MathML in its HTML output alongside the visual rendering. **How academics actually render math.** Terry Tao: WordPress LaTeX plugin → **images** (dated, but it works and survives forever). Scott Aaronson: also embedded images. Ciechanowski: inline and display math rendered in-page (e.g. `F = G × m1 × m2 / r²`). Distill: proper typeset math with numbered citations. **Citations.** Terry Tao links to zbMATH and arXiv, and cross-references his own prior posts extensively. Distill: numbered inline citations `[1]` → a References block, plus a "Citations and Reuse" section carrying plain text + BibTeX + CC licence + GitHub source, and a DOI. RealClimate embeds scholarly rigor (NOAA declarations, CMIP simulations, named datasets) without a formal bibliography, translating peer review into public language: *"A new paper undermines totally inaccurate claims in the DOE report."* **Dark mode + figures.** This is the trap. Gwern's solution is **per-image AI classification via InvertOrNot.com** to decide whether an image can be safely inverted — an admission that blanket inversion is destructive. macwright.com uses an auto light/dark toggle. Ciechanowski's interactive canvases draw their own backgrounds, so the question doesn't arise for him. For matplotlib PNGs (which is what hydrology figures are), the light-plate approach is the only robust answer. --- ## 6. Voice and framing — concrete specimens **Titles (verified):** - "A Recipe for Training Neural Networks" — Karpathy - "Against 'Brain Damage'" (subtitle: "AI can help, or hurt, our thinking") — Mollick - "Has groundwater finally gone mainstream?" — EGU HS - "Summary of the August 26th, 2026, Himalayan flash flood" — EGU HS - "eDNA4Hydrology" — EGU HS - "The world of tomorrow" (dek: "When the future arrived, it felt… ordinary. What happened to the glamour of tomorrow?") — Works in Progress - "Factories are just rooms" — Matt Webb - "Staring into the abyss as a core life skill" — Ben Kuhn - "A Swarm of Blood Robots" (dek: "Recent adventures using LLMs") — Craig Mod **Openings (verified):** - Karpathy: *"Some few weeks ago I posted a tweet…"* — provenance, not hook. - Aaronson: *"I woke up yesterday with the following thoughts, which are probably either obvious or dumb."* — pre-emptive self-deprecation as a credibility move. - Mollick: acknowledges the widespread concern, then immediately reframes — *"not because AI causes literal brain damage (it doesn't) but because the question itself shows how deeply we fear what AI might do to our ability to think."* - Asterisk dek: *"Once you realize what that means, you'll be giving two cheers for the American work ethic"* — frames, does not summarize. - RealClimate on an El Niño: *"both unusually early in the year and very soon since the last El Niño"* — relatable temporal markers instead of jargon. - RealClimate comment policy: *"Please be constructive and keep nonsense to a minimum."* **Anti-marketing signals that recur:** stated uncertainty; a named lower-quality tier ("Rough Notes"); explicit scope modesty (Nadia's "little pied-à-terre"); no CTA inside the body; conversational asides (Craig Mod's *"Whacked together by Craig Mod since 2002"*). --- ## 7. Concrete proposed structure for satishregonda.in ### Routes ``` /writing/ index (list, no pagination until ~30 posts) /writing// post /writing/kind// four kind pages (explainer|comment|field-note|for-students) /writing/archive/ year-grouped list — SHIP LATER (~25 posts) /writing/tags// SHIP LATER (~15 posts) /feed.xml Atom, day one /feed.json JSON Feed, day one (cheap) ``` ### Index — 0 posts (should never ship, but if forced) No ghost cards, no "Coming soon", no skeleton. The page becomes a **statement of intent**: 1. Page title "Writing" + a 2–3 sentence standfirst in his voice, e.g. *"Notes on rivers, monsoons, and the floods we keep being surprised by. Mostly written after a field trip or an argument."* 2. The four kinds, each with one descriptive sentence — this alone occupies the visual space three entries would. 3. "In the meantime" — 4–6 links out: recent papers, RAFT, a talk video, a press piece. 4. Footer: RSS + email, with the honest line "A few times a year." ### Index — 3 posts (the target state) ``` WRITING Notes on rivers, monsoons, and the floods we keep being surprised by. ← standfirst, 2 lines, 20px muted ────────────────────────────────────────────────── EXPLAINER 14 Mar 2026 Hyderabad's floods are a forecasting failure, not a drainage failure ← 32px serif Why we keep building bigger drains for a problem that is mostly about the twelve hours before rain. ← dek, 18px muted ────────────────────────────────────────────────── FOR STUDENTS 02 Feb 2026 What I look for in a PhD applicant The honest version, including the parts I usually soften in email. ────────────────────────────────────────────────── FIELD NOTE 11 Jan 2026 Three days on the Musi Photographs and gauge readings from a river that is mostly sewage and occasionally a flood. ────────────────────────────────────────────────── WHAT I WRITE ABOUT HERE Explainer — turning a paper into something a city engineer can act on. Comment — opinions on water policy and practice in India, held loosely. Field note — what a place looks like when you stand in it, with the data. For students — advice I repeat often enough that it should be written down. ELSEWHERE Peer-reviewed papers → RAFT research group → Talks → Teaching → Subscribe by email · RSS · A few times a year. ``` That is roughly 1.5 screens of deliberate, authored content with three posts. It reads as an editor's page, not a stalled CMS. ### Index — ~15 posts (the evolution) Drop the standfirst to one line; shrink titles to 24px; drop the "What I write about here" block (the kinds become filter links in a single row); introduce year separators; add the tags page. ### Post page anatomy ``` ← Writing [breadcrumb, 14px sans] EXPLAINER [kind label, 11px caps sans] Hyderabad's floods are a forecasting [42px serif, tight] failure, not a drainage failure Why we keep building bigger drains for a [22px muted serif italic — dek] problem that is mostly about the twelve hours before rain. Satish Regonda · 14 March 2026 · 2,300 words [14px sans, muted, hairline under] ┌─ Based on ───────────────────────────────┐ [callout, only on Explainers] │ Regonda, S.K. et al. (2025). Title. │ │ Journal of Hydrology 640, 131234. │ │ DOI: 10.1016/… · PDF │ └──────────────────────────────────────────┘ [body, 66ch, 19–20px serif, 1.6, ragged right] h2 sections; h3 sparingly sidenotes into right margin ≥1200px Fig. 1 — captions 14px sans muted figures on light plates in both themes KaTeX display math, build-time References [numbered, DOI links] Cite this post ▸ [collapsed: plain text + BibTeX] ────────────────────────────────────────────── Also here What I look for in a PhD applicant → Three days on the Musi → Subscribe · RSS ``` ### The four kinds → template variations (so the site doesn't feel uniform) - **Explainer** — has the "Based on" callout, References block, "Cite this post", and usually figures. The most formal template. - **Comment** — no callout, no references; allows a single epigraph at the top; shorter measure feels right; dek does more work. - **Field note** — image-forward. Full-bleed photographs with margin captions; optionally a small location line ("Musi River, Hyderabad · 17.36°N 78.47°E"); no math. - **For students** — allows an explicit TOC even when short, because it will be linked to and re-read; allows numbered lists; no citation apparatus. ### Google Docs authoring contract (blog-specific) Front-matter table at the head of each Doc: | Field | Value | |---|---| | Title | Hyderabad's floods are a forecasting failure, not a drainage failure | | Dek | Why we keep building bigger drains for a problem that is mostly about the twelve hours before rain. | | Date | 2026-03-14 | | Kind | Explainer | | Tags | urban-flooding, forecasting | | Slug | hyderabad-forecasting-failure | | Status | Published | Mappings: Docs Heading 1 → `h2`; Heading 2 → `h3`; **Docs footnotes → sidenotes**; image + following paragraph in the "Caption" style → `

exemplars.name: Andrej Karpathy — Stanford / OpenAI (personal blog)
exemplars.what_works: One page, reverse-chron, ~40 posts, zero pagination. Each entry is exactly date + title + one authored line of description. No tags, no search, no reading time, no cards. The whole design decision is 'the titles and the deks carry it', and they do. RSS at /feed.xml is the only affordance.
exemplars.steal_this: The three-element entry — date, title, one authored line — as the atomic unit of the index. This is the form we should ship, because it looks identical whether there are 3 entries or 40.

exemplars.name: Craig Mod — independent writer/photographer
exemplars.what_works: 70+ essays 2009–2026 in a single reverse-chron list, with a separate 'Popular Essays' block of four placed next to the newsletter signup. Descriptions are conversational and specific ('Returning to drumming after a fourteen-year break'), never summary-shaped. Newsletter copy is disarming: 'Always one-click to unsub.'
exemplars.steal_this: A small 'Popular / Start here' block of 3–4 essays sitting beside the subscribe form — it gives newcomers a path and gives the subscribe form a reason to exist without being a popup.

exemplars.name: Ben Kuhn — Anthropic (personal essays)
exemplars.what_works: Featured essays first, ~10 of them, with NO dates shown on the index — an explicit bet on timelessness. Recent posts are demoted to a secondary list. Each post ends with a hand-picked 'Related' trio, each carrying a one-line tagline. Long essays open with a hierarchical in-page TOC.
exemplars.steal_this: Suppressing dates on the index for an essay-shaped, low-frequency blog. A hydrology explainer from 2026 is not stale in 2029, and hiding the date removes the single strongest 'this blog is dormant' signal.

exemplars.name: Bartosz Ciechanowski — independent (interactive explainers)
exemplars.what_works: Roughly one post a year, and the site never reads as abandoned. Enormous per-post depth, a clean dated finish line, interactive figures placed full-width inline in the prose (never in a sidebar), with the caption text placed BEFORE the demo to prime the reader. No tags, no read time, no share row, no comments.
exemplars.steal_this: Caption-before-figure for anything the reader has to interpret (a hydrograph, a flood-extent map). It turns a figure from decoration into an instruction, and it is the correct move for a scientific audience.

exemplars.name: Edward Tufte / Dave Liepmann — Tufte CSS
exemplars.what_works: A complete, documented system: #fffff8 on #111111, ETBook with Palatino/Georgia fallback, exactly three heading levels justified by the Feynman Lectures, JS-free sidenotes via a label+checkbox+span pattern that collapses gracefully on mobile, and three figure classes (main-column, margin, .fullwidth).
exemplars.steal_this: The label/checkbox sidenote pattern verbatim, plus the three-heading-level rule. It gives us a distinctive, scholarly layout with no JavaScript and it maps perfectly onto Google Docs' native footnote feature — which the professor already knows how to use.

exemplars.name: Gwern Branwen — independent researcher
exemplars.what_works: Every design choice is stated with a reason: Source Serif Pro / Source Sans Pro / IBM Plex Mono (chosen after blind comparison of ~20 code fonts because of the slashed zero), sidenotes.js promoting footnotes to margin notes only when the window is wide enough, and dark mode using per-image AI classification (InvertOrNot.com) to decide whether inversion is safe. Stated principles: minimalism, progressive enhancement with no JS required for reading, speed, semantic zoom.
exemplars.steal_this: The per-image dark-mode decision — but implemented cheaply, by giving every scientific figure a permanent light 'plate' instead of inverting. That admission (that blanket inversion breaks figures) is the most useful single finding for a site full of matplotlib output.

exemplars.name: Distill (Chris Olah, Shan Carter et al.)
exemplars.what_works: Narrow centred text column (~600–800px) with figures escaping to full viewport width; numbered inline citations resolving to a References block; author + affiliation + date byline; and a 'Citations and Reuse' section carrying plain-text citation, BibTeX, CC licence and a GitHub source link, with a DOI.
exemplars.steal_this: The 'Cite this post' block with plain text + BibTeX, collapsed by default. It costs nothing, almost no personal site has it, and it signals to other academics that the writing is meant to be referenced.

exemplars.name: Simon Willison — independent (Datasette)
exemplars.what_works: 1,000+ tags with live counts, tag intersections at /tags/tag1+tag2/, year archives 2002–2026, Atom declared in the head, and — crucially — WORD COUNTS instead of reading times on index entries ('[2,270 words]'). Content is split into distinct streams: Entries, Links, Quotes, Notes.
exemplars.steal_this: Word count instead of reading time, and the stream split. We should split 'Writing' (essays) from 'News' (one-line group updates), so the essays never get diluted by 'our paper was accepted'.

exemplars.name: Chris Olah — Anthropic (personal blog)
exemplars.what_works: ~30–40 posts grouped by subject domain rather than date, each with a thumbnail and a descriptive subtitle. A named 'Rough Notes' tier for lower-polish work, with the reason stated ('polishing takes lots of time'), and a 'Traditional Papers' list at the bottom that grounds the blog inside formal academic output.
exemplars.steal_this: The named lower tier. Giving the professor a legitimate place to put a 400-word half-thought — labelled as such — is what will actually keep the blog alive between the two or three essays a year he has time to polish.

exemplars.name: EGU Blogs — Hydrological Sciences Division
exemplars.what_works: The closest disciplinary analogue: 34 categories (groundwater, catchment hydrology, extreme events, hydrological forecasting, remote sensing, water policy), author + date + featured image + excerpt, and post types that map exactly onto our brief — event explainers ('Summary of the August 26th, 2026, Himalayan flash flood'), method notes ('eDNA4Hydrology'), and field-of-view opinion ('Has groundwater finally gone mainstream?'). Field photographs are captioned with location and credit.
exemplars.steal_this: The post-type taxonomy and the titling register. 'Has groundwater finally gone mainstream?' is exactly the tone we want — a real question from inside the field, not a benefit promise.

exemplars.name: RealClimate — working climate scientists, collective blog
exemplars.what_works: A 'Start here' item in the primary nav for newcomers; a recurring monthly open thread ('Unforced Variations') that guarantees a heartbeat regardless of essay output; date + author + comment count; footer sections for 'Data and Graphics', 'Index' and 'Acronym Index'; and a stated comment norm ('Please be constructive and keep nonsense to a minimum'). Scientists translate peer review into plain public language.
exemplars.steal_this: 'Start here' in the nav, and the idea of one recurring low-effort series that fires on a schedule — for us, something like a short seasonal monsoon note — so the blog has a floor of activity that does not depend on inspiration.

exemplars.name: Works in Progress — magazine
exemplars.what_works: Issue number stamped at the top, large centred typographic headline with no hero image, byline + date + share + translate, and a dek that poses the article's question rather than summarising it ('When the future arrived, it felt… ordinary. What happened to the glamour of tomorrow?'). Serif body, sans headers, images inline with terse source-only captions, substantive numbered footnotes at the end.
exemplars.steal_this: The typographic headline with no hero image. It reads more serious than any stock photo could, and it costs nothing — which matters when the author has no image budget and no designer.

exemplars.name: Julia Evans — independent
exemplars.what_works: Post pages carry only a date and ONE category tag at the top. ~950px column, h1 title with h3 sections, prev/next at the foot, no comments, and the newsletter offer placed mid-page rather than as a modal or a sticky bar. The index shows 'Most recent 10 posts' then ~20 thematic groupings with ★ on the popular ones.
exemplars.steal_this: One tag maximum at the top of a post, and the mid-page rather than modal subscribe. Also the ★ convention — a single glyph is a cheaper 'featured' mechanism than a whole curated section when the archive is small.

exemplars.name: Matt Webb — Interconnected
exemplars.what_works: Archive by year 2000–2026 WITH per-year post counts, 'Best of' collections for newcomers, an 'On this day' feature that mines the archive, and both Buttondown email and RSS presented side by side each with an explainer link for readers who don't know what RSS is.
exemplars.steal_this: The explainer link next to the RSS icon. Academic readers span a huge range of technical comfort; a one-line 'what is this?' next to the feed link is the difference between an icon and a subscriber.

exemplars.name: Scott Aaronson — UT Austin, Shtetl-Optimized
exemplars.what_works: A professor's blog that has run since 2005: full posts on the index, date + categories + comment count, and a sidebar carrying monthly archives, 30+ categories, a blogroll, lecture notes, and a 'The Basics' block linking CV, papers, talks and home page. Openings are self-deprecating and unguarded ('I woke up yesterday with the following thoughts, which are probably either obvious or dumb').
exemplars.steal_this: The 'The Basics' sidebar block — CV, papers, talks — placed on the blog itself. On an academic site the blog is often the entry point from social media, so it should always offer a one-click route back to the formal record.

pitfalls: Shipping an empty /writing page with 'Coming soon', a ghost skeleton card, or a placeholder illustration. Nothing signals 'abandoned template' faster. Seed three real posts before launch or make the index an editorial statement page instead.

A card grid with generic gradient thumbnails, abstract stock photos, or AI-generated hero images. This is the single strongest AI-template tell in 2026. The only reference site with a credible card index (Maggie Appleton) draws her own illustrations for every essay.

The media-company costume: reading-time-in-minutes + a scroll progress bar + a social share row + a sticky subscribe bar. Zero of the ~25 personal and academic sites I fetched have all four. Digiday documents that designers find progress bars distracting and readers confuse them with loading bars.

Putting the blog on Substack. It moves the writing off satishregonda.in, wraps a professor's prose in another company's branding, and imports restack/paywall/subscriber-count furniture. Ethan Mollick's index leads with a subscribe wall and a 'No thanks' dismissal before you can read anything — that is Substack's design, not his.

Auto-inverting figures in dark mode. Gwern needed a per-image AI classifier precisely because blanket inversion destroys images. Hydrology figures are overwhelmingly white-background matplotlib PNGs; inverted, a blue-to-red streamflow colormap becomes actively misleading.

A tag cloud, a search box, an archive page, or pagination over three posts. Each one is a UI element with nothing behind it, and each makes the emptiness measurable. Defer them to ~15 / ~40 / ~25 / ~30 posts respectively.

Loading MathJax's runtime for two equations a year. Render KaTeX at build time and ship zero math JavaScript. (Also avoid Terry Tao's WordPress-LaTeX-as-images approach — it doesn't scale, doesn't select, and doesn't survive dark mode.)

Disqus or any third-party comment embed. Karpathy has it and it is the one blemish on an otherwise clean site: third-party tracking, ads, and threads that die. Julia Evans, Dan Luu, Ciechanowski, Olah, Craig Mod and Ben Kuhn all run without comments. A 'corrections and disagreements: <email>' line is more in keeping.

Auto-generated excerpts (first N words) in place of authored deks. This is the difference between Craig Mod's index and a default Jekyll theme. Make Dek a REQUIRED field in the Google Doc front-matter and refuse to build without it.

Letting the blog absorb group news. If 'our paper was accepted' and 'congratulations to X on her defence' land in the same stream as the essays, the essays stop reading as essays within about six months. Route news to a separate dated ticker driven from a Sheet.

Date-stamped URLs (/writing/2026/03/14/slug/) on a four-posts-a-year blog. Every shared link and every search result will advertise how long ago he last wrote. Undated slugs with the date shown on the page give the same information without the staleness cue.
Justified text. It is the reflex of anyone who writes in LaTeX, and in a browser without proper hyphenation and justification it produces rivers of whitespace at a 66ch measure. Set ragged right.

More than two typeface families, or a display face for headlines. A serif for body plus a sans for labels and captions is the entire system in every reference site worth copying. Gwern uses three only because the third is a code font chosen on a specific technical criterion.

Decorative pull quotes lifted out of the body. A magazine device that, on a single-author academic site, reads as padding — and it is padding, since it repeats text the reader is about to encounter. An epigraph at the head of a piece is the acceptable version.

Scroll-triggered fade-ins, parallax, or animated counters. Gwern's stated principle is that core reading requires no JavaScript at all; every reference site meets that bar. Motion on an academic blog reads as a template's default settings left on.

Building the four post kinds as visually identical pages. If an Explainer, a field note and a piece of student advice all render with the same furniture (citation block, references, TOC), the taxonomy is decoration. Vary the templates so a field note is image-forward and citation-free and an explainer carries the full academic apparatus.

Relying on a link to raftwaters.in without verifying it. That domain did not resolve when I tried it (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND) — confirm it is live and pointed correctly before the RAFT page ships with an outbound link to it.
